learning_target: Students will explain that motion is relative and describe an object’s motion using an appropriate frame of reference.
i_can: I can explain why an object can be moving relative to one reference frame but not another.
expected_evidence: At rest relative to the belt; moving east relative to the floor tile. Naming “relative to” a reference frame makes the statements complete.
rubric_reference: Course progress language: Not Yet / Approaching / Meeting / Exceeding

learning_target: Students will explain that motion is relative and describe an object’s motion using an appropriate frame of reference.
i_can: I can identify the reference frame used in a motion description.
expected_evidence: They use different reference frames: the train frame makes the post move west; the station/Earth frame makes the train move east.
rubric_reference: Course progress language: Not Yet / Approaching / Meeting / Exceeding

learning_target: Students will explain that motion is relative and describe an object’s motion using an appropriate frame of reference.
i_can: I can compare motion from two different points of view and explain why everyday motion is usually described relative to Earth’s surface.
expected_evidence: Displacement is -8 m (8 m left). Example: The robot moved 8 m left relative to the doorway.
rubric_reference: Course progress language: Not Yet / Approaching / Meeting / Exceeding

learning_target: Students will distinguish between speed and velocity and use distance, time, and direction to describe motion.
i_can: I can calculate average speed from distance and time.
practice_standard: quantitative reasoning; data interpretation; communication with units
expected_evidence: 7 m/s; velocity also needs direction.
rubric_reference: Course progress language: Not Yet / Approaching / Meeting / Exceeding

learning_target: Students will distinguish between speed and velocity and use distance, time, and direction to describe motion.
i_can: I can distinguish instantaneous speed from average speed.
practice_standard: quantitative reasoning; data interpretation; communication with units
expected_evidence: Distance 120 m; average speed 8 m/s. Average velocity requires displacement with direction.
rubric_reference: Course progress language: Not Yet / Approaching / Meeting / Exceeding

learning_target: Students will distinguish between speed and velocity and use distance, time, and direction to describe motion.
i_can: I can explain that velocity includes both speed and direction and compare examples of constant speed, constant velocity, and changing velocity.
practice_standard: quantitative reasoning; data interpretation; communication with units
expected_evidence: No. Interval speeds are 4 m/s, 6 m/s, and 8 m/s.
rubric_reference: Course progress language: Not Yet / Approaching / Meeting / Exceeding

learning_target: Students will explain acceleration as the rate at which velocity changes and identify acceleration from motion descriptions, data, and graphs.
i_can: I can calculate acceleration from change in velocity and time.
practice_standard: graph/data interpretation; quantitative reasoning; model translation
expected_evidence: Acceleration +2 m/s^2; it slows because speed decreases from 10 to 2 m/s.
rubric_reference: Course progress language: Not Yet / Approaching / Meeting / Exceeding

learning_target: Students will explain acceleration as the rate at which velocity changes and identify acceleration from motion descriptions, data, and graphs.
i_can: I can explain that acceleration can involve speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction.
practice_standard: graph/data interpretation; quantitative reasoning; model translation
expected_evidence: Yes. Direction changes, so velocity changes even though speed remains 6 m/s.
rubric_reference: Course progress language: Not Yet / Approaching / Meeting / Exceeding

learning_target: Students will explain acceleration as the rate at which velocity changes and identify acceleration from motion descriptions, data, and graphs.
i_can: I can identify positive, negative, or zero acceleration from a motion situation and interpret simple motion graphs and connect them to velocity or acceleration.
practice_standard: graph/data interpretation; quantitative reasoning; model translation
expected_evidence: Acceleration +2 m/s^2. Crossing v=0 means the object is momentarily at rest and reverses direction.
rubric_reference: Course progress language: Not Yet / Approaching / Meeting / Exceeding

learning_target: Students will describe free fall as motion under the influence of gravity alone and use simple free-fall relationships to determine speed or distance fallen.
i_can: I can explain why objects in free fall accelerate at the same rate when air resistance is ignored.
practice_standard: mathematical reasoning; model evaluation; explanation of phenomena
expected_evidence: Speed 30 m/s; distance 45 m. Speed is proportional to t, while distance from rest is proportional to t^2.
rubric_reference: Course progress language: Not Yet / Approaching / Meeting / Exceeding

learning_target: Students will describe free fall as motion under the influence of gravity alone and use simple free-fall relationships to determine speed or distance fallen.
i_can: I can use $g \approx 10\text{ m/s}^2$ to determine speed gained during free fall.
practice_standard: mathematical reasoning; model evaluation; explanation of phenomena
expected_evidence: They fall together with the same acceleration because gravity produces the same free-fall acceleration when air resistance is absent.
rubric_reference: Course progress language: Not Yet / Approaching / Meeting / Exceeding

learning_target: Students will describe free fall as motion under the influence of gravity alone and use simple free-fall relationships to determine speed or distance fallen.
i_can: I can use free-fall patterns to compare distance fallen during different time intervals and distinguish free fall from falling with significant air resistance.
practice_standard: mathematical reasoning; model evaluation; explanation of phenomena

rubric_reference: Course progress language: Not Yet / Approaching / Meeting / Exceeding
